title: A Model for the Structural, Functional, and Deontic Specification of Organizations in Multiagent Systems (MOISE+)
authors_or_lab: Jomi Fred Hübner, Jaime Simão Sichman, Olivier Boissier (USP / École des Mines de Saint-Étienne)
venue_year: SBIA 2002, Springer LNAI 2507, pp. 118–128 (also AAMAS 2002 short paper)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Springer LNAI conference proceedings (SBIA); the companion short paper is in AAMAS 2002. Foundational, ~1500+ citations, and the direct ancestor of the Moise organisational engine in JaCaMo.
what_it_establishes: Splits an organisation specification into exactly three orthogonal dimensions: STRUCTURAL (roles, inheritance between roles, three link types — acquaintance, communication, authority — plus groups with role cardinality/compatibility constraints), FUNCTIONAL (a global goal decomposition tree, partitioned into missions, each mission a coherent bundle of goals), and DEONTIC (the only bridge between the two: a set of permissions and obligations of the form <role, mission, time-constraint>). Permission = may commit to the mission; obligation = must. Nothing else in the model creates duty. Explicitly designed so that structure and function can be authored and changed independently while the deontic layer stays a small, auditable join table.
use_in_consilient: This is literally the schema behind RACI, done properly and 24 years earlier. Our RACI matrix is MOISE+'s deontic specification with a poorer type system: <role, mission, deontic-operator> is <role, deliverable, R/A/C/I>. Adopt the three-dimension split for the agent-org spec: structure (who exists, who may talk to whom, who has authority over whom) must be a separate artefact from function (goal tree / mission decomposition), joined only by an explicit permission/obligation table. Also adopt link typing — our dependency matrix currently conflates 'can see', 'can message' and 'can direct', which MOISE+ separates as acquaintance/communication/authority.
the_bar_it_sets: An org spec must be decomposable into three independently-editable specs whose join is a finite, enumerable deontic relation. We beat it by showing our deontic table is (a) machine-checkable against the structural spec (no obligation on a role that cannot reach the resource), and (b) empirically enforced at runtime — i.e. measured violation counts, which MOISE+ itself did not report.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for DOI 10.1007/3-540-36127-8_12 returned exact title, all three authors, LNCS/Advances in AI container, pages 118-128, year 2002. Note: I did NOT confirm a single canonical DOI for the AAMAS'02 short paper — CrossRef returns two competing ids (10.1145/544741.544858 and 10.1145/544852.544858), so cite the LNAI chapter, not the AAMAS one.

title: Instrumenting Multi-Agent Organisations with Organisational Artifacts and Agents (ORA4MAS)
authors_or_lab: Jomi F. Hübner, Olivier Boissier, Rosine Kitio, Alessandro Ricci (Mines Saint-Étienne / Univ. of Bologna)
reputable_because: JAAMAS is the flagship peer-reviewed journal of the AAMAS community (Springer, IFAAMAS-affiliated).
what_it_establishes: Answers the question every org model dodges: WHO ENFORCES IT. Reifies the organisation as first-class runtime entities — organisational artifacts (GroupBoard, SchemeBoard, NormativeBoard) that agents perceive and act on — and distinguishes two enforcement regimes: REGIMENTATION (the artifact makes the violating action physically impossible; zero autonomy, zero violation) versus REGULATION (the action is possible, the violation is detected and reported to a designated organisational agent who applies sanctions). The choice is made per-norm, not per-system, so a single organisation can hard-block some actions and merely audit others.
use_in_consilient: This is our autonomy-levels axis, already formalised. Map each of our autonomy levels onto the regimentation/regulation dial per capability: L0 = regimented (tool call physically unavailable), L3 = regulated (call permitted, logged, sanctioned on violation). Adopt the organisational-artifact pattern for the accountability substrate: the org state must live in an observable, inspectable object the agents act on, not in prompt text — prompt-only norms cannot be regimented and cannot be audited.
the_bar_it_sets: Every norm in the system must be classified regimented vs regulated, and for regulated norms there must be a detector and a named accountable agent. We beat it by reporting the detection rate for regulated norms (ORA4MAS assumes detection is perfect because the artifact mediates every action; with LLM agents and out-of-band channels it is not — so measured detection recall is the number that shows we surpassed it).

title: Multi-agent oriented programming with JaCaMo
authors_or_lab: Olivier Boissier, Rafael H. Bordini, Jomi F. Hübner, Alessandro Ricci, Andrea Santi (Mines Saint-Étienne / PUCRS / UFSC / Bologna)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Elsevier journal; the paper defines the reference implementation used across two decades of AAMAS work, and the follow-on MIT-Press-style textbook 'Multi-Agent Oriented Programming' (2020).
what_it_establishes: The only mature stack that runs all three levels simultaneously: Jason (agent level — BDI plans, beliefs, goals), CArtAgO (environment level — artifacts as shared, observable, operable state), and Moise (organisation level — the MOISE+ spec above, live and modifiable at runtime). The contribution is the semantic glue: an agent adopting a role acquires the mission obligations as goals, and organisational changes propagate into agent goal bases without restarting the system.
use_in_consilient: The layering is the architectural prior we should copy: agent / environment / organisation as three separately-programmed, separately-inspectable layers rather than one prompt. Our tool-surface is CArtAgO's environment layer; our RACI+autonomy spec is Moise's organisation layer; the model is the agent layer. Naming these boundaries explicitly gives us three independent measurement points instead of one end-to-end score.
the_bar_it_sets: An organisation must be changeable at runtime and have that change take effect in agent behaviour without a restart. Measurement that beats it: time-to-effect and correctness of a live RACI/autonomy change (does the agent actually stop doing the thing within N actions of the norm changing?) — JaCaMo demonstrates the mechanism but publishes no such latency/compliance numbers.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1016/j.scico.2011.10.004 returned exact title, five authors, Science of Computer Programming vol 78 pp 747-761, 2013.

title: A meta-model for the analysis and design of organizations in multi-agent systems (Aalaadin / AGR)
authors_or_lab: Jacques Ferber, Olivier Gutknecht (LIRMM, Univ. Montpellier)
venue_year: ICMAS 1998 (3rd Int. Conf. on Multi-Agent Systems), IEEE, pp. 128–135
reputable_because: ICMAS was the peer-reviewed predecessor conference to AAMAS; this is the origin paper of the Agent/Group/Role model (MadKit platform) and one of the two or three most-cited organisational MAS papers ever.
what_it_establishes: The minimal organisational ontology: exactly three primitives — AGENT (an active entity with an identity, deliberately left as a black box with no assumed internal architecture), GROUP (a set of agents; the unit of scoping — agents can only interact with agents in a shared group), and ROLE (an abstract representation of a function, played by an agent within a group; an agent may hold several roles and belong to several groups). Organisational structure is thus a bipartite graph of agents to (group, role) pairs. Crucially: agent identity is separate from role identity, and the group is the boundary of visibility and communication.
use_in_consilient: Fixes our agent-identity problem at the root. AGR's discipline is that a message is addressed to a ROLE IN A GROUP, not to an agent — so agent instances become fungible and replaceable without rewriting the org. Adopt: identity = stable agent id; capability and duty = attached to (group, role) tuples the identity holds; visibility = group membership, which is also the natural scope for our dependency matrix (an entry outside a shared group is a spec error, statically detectable).
the_bar_it_sets: Foundational, and absent from our bibliography — this is the 25-year blind spot in its purest form. The bar: a system where communication is role-addressed and group-scoped, so an agent can be swapped mid-run with no edit to the organisation. We beat it by measuring substitution: replace an agent instance holding a role and show task outcome unchanged, which AGR asserts as a design property but never measured.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1109/ICMAS.1998.699041 returned exact title, authors Ferber J. and Gutknecht O., ICMAS'98 proceedings, pages 128-135.

title: The Gaia Methodology for Agent-Oriented Analysis and Design
authors_or_lab: Michael Wooldridge, Nicholas R. Jennings, David Kinny (Oxford / Southampton / Melbourne)
reputable_because: JAAMAS, peer-reviewed; authors are Oxford (Wooldridge) and then-Southampton (Jennings) — both on any definition of top-tier. 2000+ citations. Extended as 'Developing multiagent systems: The Gaia methodology', ACM TOSEM 12(3), 2003, DOI 10.1145/958961.958963.
what_it_establishes: Treats a MAS as a computational ORGANISATION and gives the role schema its canonical four slots: RESPONSIBILITIES (split into liveness properties — things the role must bring about — and safety properties — invariants the role must never violate), PERMISSIONS (the resources the role is entitled to read/change, stated as rights over named information), ACTIVITIES (private computations), and PROTOCOLS (interactions with other roles). Plus an explicit acquaintance model capturing which roles communicate with which — the ancestor of the dependency matrix.
use_in_consilient: Gives our RACI rows the fields they are currently missing. A role definition that lists only 'responsible for X' is half a spec: Gaia insists you also name the permissions (which files, tools, data the role may touch) and the safety invariants (what it must never do). Adopt the liveness/safety split directly — it maps onto 'the deliverable' vs 'the guardrail', and safety properties are exactly what an autonomy level should regiment. The acquaintance model is our dependency matrix, and Gaia's rule that it be derived from the protocol set gives us a consistency check.
the_bar_it_sets: Every role must carry responsibilities (liveness AND safety), permissions over named resources, and protocols — and the acquaintance graph must be derivable from the protocols rather than asserted separately. Beating it: show our acquaintance/dependency matrix is machine-derived from actual observed message traffic and matches the declared one, i.e. a measured spec-conformance number Gaia (a paper methodology) never produced.

title: On the Formal Specification of Electronic Institutions
authors_or_lab: Marc Esteva, Juan-Antonio Rodríguez-Aguilar, Carles Sierra, Pere Garcia, Josep L. Arcos (IIIA-CSIC, Barcelona)
venue_year: Agent Mediated Electronic Commerce, Springer LNAI 1991, pp. 126–147, 2001
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Springer LNAI; IIIA-CSIC is the institution that created the Electronic Institutions line, and this is its formal-foundations paper. The runtime is AMELI (AAMAS 2004) and the engineering account is Arcos et al., Engineering Applications of AI 18(2), 2005, DOI 10.1016/j.engappai.2004.11.019.
what_it_establishes: Institutions as enforced interaction protocols rather than advisory norms. Four primitives: DIALOGIC FRAMEWORK (the shared ontology and illocutions — what can even be said), SCENES (a scene is a finite-state protocol among roles, with defined entry/exit states per role), PERFORMATIVE STRUCTURE (a network of scenes with the legal transitions of agents between them, including role-change and synchronisation), and NORMS (commitments incurred by uttering an illocution — obligations that become due in later scenes). Roles are institutional, an agent adopts one at entry, and the institution mediates every utterance so that illegal actions are simply not admitted.
use_in_consilient: The strongest available prior for accountability that actually binds. Two things to steal: (1) commitments incurred by speech acts — when an agent says 'I will deliver X', that becomes a tracked obligation with a deadline and a scene where it comes due, which is exactly the accountability half of RACI's 'A'; (2) mediation — the institution sits in the message path, so 'permitted' is enforced rather than requested. Our tool broker should be an AMELI-style governor, not a policy document in the system prompt.
the_bar_it_sets: Illegal actions must be impossible, not merely discouraged, and every commitment must have a scene where it is discharged or breached. We beat it by handling what EI cannot: LLM agents whose 'illocutions' are unconstrained natural language. The measurement that shows it: rate at which free-text commitments are correctly extracted into tracked obligations, and breach detection rate — EI gets 100% by fiat because the language is finite; we have to earn a number.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1007/3-540-44682-6_8 returned exact title, all five authors, LNCS/Agent Mediated Electronic Commerce, pp 126-147, 2001. I also saw IIIA-CSIC's own hosted PDFs for the AMELI middleware paper at iiia.csic.es.

title: OperettA: Organization-Oriented Development Environment (the OperA model and its tool)
authors_or_lab: Huib Aldewereld, Virginia Dignum (Utrecht University / TU Delft)
venue_year: Languages, Methodologies, and Development Tools for Multi-Agent Systems (LADS), Springer LNCS 6822, pp. 1–18, 2011
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Springer LNCS post-proceedings of the LADS workshop at MALLOW; Dignum's OperA is one of the two dominant European organisational frameworks. The formal core is 'A logic of agent organizations', Dignum & Dignum, Logic Journal of IGPL 20(1):283–316, 2011, DOI 10.1093/jigpal/jzr041 (verified separately).
what_it_establishes: OperA's defining move is the separation of the ORGANISATIONAL MODEL (roles with objectives, rights, norms; interaction scenes; the social structure the designer owns) from the SOCIAL MODEL (social contracts between the organisation and each concrete agent, negotiated at entry) and the INTERACTION MODEL (contracts between agents). Because the agent signs a contract, it keeps its own goals and is not assumed to be a compliant component — the organisation states WHAT must be achieved, the agent decides HOW. Objectives are stated as landmark patterns (partially-ordered states) rather than plans, precisely so the agent retains discretion. The IGPL logic paper adds formal notions of role responsibility versus ability, and of organisational structure as dependencies among roles.
use_in_consilient: Gives us the contract abstraction for autonomy levels: an agent's autonomy is not a global dial but a per-engagement social contract stating objectives (landmarks), rights, and norms — renegotiable at role-adoption time. Also gives the right target formulation: specify the landmark states a deliverable must pass through, not the steps, then measure landmark attainment. That is a far better accountability signal than step-by-step trace matching.
the_bar_it_sets: An organisation spec must be satisfiable by agents with their own objectives, and must state outcomes (landmarks) not procedures. Beating it: report measured autonomy — the divergence between the agent's chosen path and any prescribed path, alongside landmark attainment, showing the freedom is real and non-costly. OperA argues autonomy is preserved; it does not quantify it.
verified_how: CrossRef API records verified for both DOIs: 10.1007/978-3-642-22723-3_1 (Aldewereld & Dignum, LNCS, pp 1-18, 2011) and 10.1093/jigpal/jzr041 (Dignum & Dignum, Logic Journal of IGPL vol 20 pp 283-316). I could not verify Dignum's 2004 Utrecht PhD thesis via CrossRef, so it is not cited here.

title: A survey of multi-agent organizational paradigms
authors_or_lab: Bryan Horling, Victor Lesser (Multi-Agent Systems Lab, UMass Amherst)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Cambridge University Press journal; Lesser's UMass MAS lab is the founding US group in distributed AI. This is the standard entry point to the whole field.
what_it_establishes: Catalogues and compares the organisational paradigms available to a designer — hierarchies, holarchies, coalitions, teams, congregations, societies, federations, markets, matrix organisations, compound forms — and for each states the characteristic benefits, costs, and the conditions under which it dominates. The key claim is that organisational form is a design variable with predictable performance consequences, not a stylistic choice, and that no form is universally best.
use_in_consilient: Straight fix for a 25-year blind spot: our design space for multi-agent structure is currently 'flat' vs 'a supervisor', which is two points in a space this paper enumerates at ten. Use it as the taxonomy axis for any structural experiment we run — if we claim a structure works, we should say which of these paradigms it is and which alternatives we compared against. Matrix organisations in particular are the direct precedent for RACI's two-axis assignment.
the_bar_it_sets: Foundational and absent from our bibliography — more valuable than a recent paper for exactly the reason stated in the brief. The bar it sets is qualitative (a complete design space with predicted trade-offs); we beat it by turning the predictions into measurements — run the same task under ≥3 named paradigms from this taxonomy and report cost/quality, which the survey reasons about but does not measure.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1017/S0269888905000317 returned exact title, authors HORLING, BRYAN and LESSER, VICTOR, The Knowledge Engineering Review vol 19 pp 281-316, Dec 2004.

title: Using quantitative models to search for appropriate organizational designs (ODML)
authors_or_lab: Bryan Horling, Victor Lesser (Multi-Agent Systems Lab, UMass Amherst)
reputable_because: JAAMAS, peer-reviewed; the definitive journal treatment of ODML (the Organizational Design Modeling Language), following Horling's UMass PhD thesis on quantitative organisational modelling.
what_it_establishes: ODML makes organisational design a search problem with a scored objective. An organisation is expressed as a graph of constructs (roles, agents, resources) annotated with mathematical expressions that compute quantitative properties — communication load, response latency, redundancy, utilisation — from the structure and the environment. Candidate designs are then generated and evaluated, with pruning, so the designer can search the space of structures and predict performance before deployment rather than after.
use_in_consilient: This is the closest classical precedent to what Consilient is for: it refuses 'this org feels better' and demands a computed number per candidate structure. Adopt the pattern of a structure-to-metric model — given a proposed RACI/dependency configuration, predict expected message volume, hand-off count, and critical-path latency, then check the prediction against the run. A prediction that survives contact with the run is much stronger evidence than a post-hoc benchmark score.
the_bar_it_sets: You must be able to score a candidate organisation before running it, and search the space rather than hand-pick one design. We beat it by reporting predicted-vs-actual error for our structural metrics on real LLM-agent runs — ODML validates against simulation and a sensor-network domain, not against agents whose behaviour is stochastic natural language.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1007/s10458-007-9020-y returned exact title, Horling & Lesser, JAAMAS vol 16 pp 95-149. I also saw Horling's UMass publication page (mas.cs.umass.edu/~bhorling/pub.html) listing the ODML line of work.

title: Evolution of the GPGP/TÆMS Domain-Independent Coordination Framework
authors_or_lab: Victor Lesser, Keith Decker, Thomas Wagner, Norman Carver, Alan Garvey, Bryan Horling, Daniel Neiman, Rodion Podorozhny, M. Nagendra Prasad, Anita Raja, Regis Vincent, Ping Xuan, X.Q. Zhang (UMass Amherst MAS Lab)
venue_year: Autonomous Agents and Multi-Agent Systems (JAAMAS) 9(1–2):87–143, July 2004
reputable_because: JAAMAS, peer-reviewed; the authoritative retrospective on TÆMS and GPGP by the group that built them at UMass.
what_it_establishes: TÆMS is a domain-independent language for task structures: a task decomposition tree whose leaves are executable methods, each with a distribution over quality/cost/duration, plus — the important part — explicit NON-LOCAL EFFECTS between tasks belonging to different agents: enables, facilitates, hinders, disables, with quantified strength and delay. GPGP is the family of coordination mechanisms that read those relationships and produce commitments (do-by-deadline, deliver-result) between agents. Coordination is thus derived from the measured dependency structure of the task environment rather than fixed in the agent code.
use_in_consilient: This is our dependency matrix with types, quantities and a scheduler attached. Our current matrix records that A depends on B; TÆMS records HOW (enables = hard precedence, facilitates = soft speed-up with a quantified factor, hinders = negative interaction) and turns each into a commitment with a deadline. Adopt the typed-edge vocabulary wholesale, and adopt the rule that a coordination protocol is generated from the dependency graph rather than hand-written per team.
the_bar_it_sets: Dependencies must be typed and quantified (hard vs soft, with magnitude and delay), and commitments must be derived from them. Beating it: extract the dependency graph from observed agent traces and show the derived commitments predict actual blocking/idle time — TÆMS models the environment by hand and evaluates in simulation.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1023/B:AGNT.0000019690.28073.04 returned exact title, the full 13-author list, JAAMAS vol 9 pp 87-143, July 2004. Also confirmed the UMass TÆMS project page exists at mas.cs.umass.edu.

title: Introduction to normative multiagent systems
authors_or_lab: Guido Boella, Leendert van der Torre, Harko Verhagen (Turin / Luxembourg / Stockholm)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Springer journal; this is the agenda-setting paper of the normative MAS (NorMAS) community and the origin of the field's working definition, feeding the long-running COIN/COINE workshop series at AAMAS.
what_it_establishes: Defines a normative MAS as a system 'together with normative systems in which agents can decide whether to follow the explicitly represented norms, and the normative systems specify how and to what extent the agents can modify the norms' — i.e. norms must be (a) explicit and inspectable, (b) violable, and (c) themselves modifiable by the agents. It frames the central design tension as the 'legal' versus 'social' conception of norms (regulative rules with sanctions vs constitutive rules that create institutional facts, à la Searle's counts-as) and sets out the obligation/permission/prohibition deontic vocabulary the field standardised on.
use_in_consilient: Supplies the conceptual hygiene our permission/obligation model needs: a norm that cannot be violated is not a norm, it is a mechanism — which is precisely the regimentation/regulation distinction and therefore the top and bottom of our autonomy scale. Also the counts-as relation is what we need to make 'approved' mean something: an institutional fact created by a designated role's act, not a string in a log.
the_bar_it_sets: Norms must be explicit, violable, and separately represented from the agents that follow them. We beat it by making the norm set executable and by publishing violation and detection statistics — the NorMAS agenda is definitional and philosophical; almost none of that literature reports empirical compliance rates for real systems.
verified_how: CrossRef API record for 10.1007/s10588-006-9537-7 returned exact title, all three authors, Computational & Mathematical Organization Theory vol 12 pp 71-79, Oct 2006.

title: Decentralized approaches for self-adaptation in agent organizations
authors_or_lab: Ramachandra Kota, Nicholas Gibbins, Nicholas R. Jennings (Univ. of Southampton, Agents Group)
venue_year: ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems (TAAS) 7(1), Article 1, 2012
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed ACM Transactions journal; Jennings' Southampton group is one of the two or three leading agent labs of the period. Extends their AAMAS 2009 'Self-organising agent organisations'.
what_it_establishes: Organisational self-design without a central designer: agents hold typed relationships with each other (peer, superior-subordinate, acquaintance), each carrying a cost and a benefit, and each agent periodically evaluates local reorganisation actions — form, dissolve or change the type of a relationship, or reallocate a task — using only local information about load and interaction history. The result is that the structure converges toward one appropriate to the current task load, and the paper compares it against centralised and static baselines on task-allocation performance.
use_in_consilient: Directly relevant to whether our RACI/dependency matrix should be authored or learned. It gives a principled middle path: fix the norms and the accountability, let the relationship graph adapt under a cost model. Also gives us a baseline family — any adaptive-org claim we make should be compared against static-optimal and centralised-reorganisation baselines, which is exactly the comparison structure this paper uses.
the_bar_it_sets: Structural adaptation must be driven by an explicit cost/benefit model over typed relationships and must beat both a static organisation and a centralised reorganiser. We beat it by running that comparison with LLM agents where relationship 'cost' includes context and token cost — Kota et al. evaluate in an abstract simulated task environment, not on real workloads.

title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
authors_or_lab: Mert Cemri, Melissa Z. Pan, Shuyi Yang, Lakshya A. Agrawal, Bhavya Chopra, Rishabh Tiwari, Kurt Keutzer, Aditya Parameswaran, Dan Klein, Kannan Ramchandran, Matei Zaharia, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Ion Stoica — UC Berkeley (Sky Computing Lab / BAIR)
reputable_because: UC Berkeley Sky Computing Lab / BAIR — Stoica, Zaharia, Gonzalez, Klein, Keutzer, Ramchandran are all Berkeley faculty; this is a top-tier university lab under the stated rule. NOT in the already-cited list (the list has 2503.11926 and 2503.24228, not 2503.13657).
what_it_establishes: MAST, a failure taxonomy for LLM multi-agent systems built from 1600+ annotated execution traces across 7 popular frameworks, with 150 traces expert-annotated at inter-annotator kappa = 0.88. 14 failure modes in 3 categories: (i) system/specification design issues, (ii) inter-agent misalignment, (iii) task verification and termination. The specification category contains exactly the organisational failures the classical literature predicts — role-specification violation, step repetition, loss of conversation history — and the misalignment category contains ignored input and derailed task handoff.
use_in_consilient: This is the measurement instrument for organisational failure. Every MAST failure mode maps to a missing organisational primitive from the classics: 'disobey role specification' = no deontic enforcement (MOISE+/ORA4MAS), 'ignored other agent's input' = broken acquaintance/dependency link (Gaia/TÆMS), 'no or incorrect verification' = no accountable role (RACI's A). Use MAST as our failure-mode label set so our organisational claims are stated in a vocabulary someone else defined and can check, and use its kappa=0.88 as the annotation-quality bar for our own trace labelling.
the_bar_it_sets: 1600+ traces, 7 frameworks, 14 modes, kappa 0.88, plus an LLM-judge annotator validated against humans. To beat it we must show that adding explicit organisational structure (roles with permissions, deontic assignments, typed dependencies) reduces the rate of specific MAST modes — reporting per-mode deltas on the same taxonomy, not a single aggregate benchmark score.
verified_how: Fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13657 directly; the abstract page returned the exact title, the full 13-author Berkeley list, submission date 17 March 2025, and the abstract stating 1600+ traces, 7 frameworks, 14 modes in 3 categories, kappa=0.88. The abstract page showed no venue in the comment field, so I do not claim a conference acceptance.

title: Norm Violation Detection in Multi-Agent Systems using Large Language Models: A Pilot Study
authors_or_lab: Shawn He, Surangika Ranathunga, Stephen Cranefield, Bastin Tony Roy Savarimuthu (University of Otago / Massey University)
venue_year: COINE@AAMAS 2024 workshop, Springer LNCS post-proceedings (arXiv Mar 2024, v2 Oct 2024)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed AAMAS workshop with Springer LNCS post-proceedings — COINE (Coordination, Organizations, Institutions, Norms and Ethics) is the direct continuation of the COIN workshop line the brief asks about. Cranefield and Savarimuthu are core normative-MAS researchers. Not in the already-cited list.
what_it_establishes: The literal handover point between the two literatures: norm violation detection, which normative MAS solved symbolically with hand-written norm representations and limited extensibility, attempted instead with LLMs. 80 household scenarios covering 10 norms, ground truth from three human evaluators per story, three models compared (GPT-4, Llama 2 7B, Mixtral). GPT-4 performs strongly, the small open models lag badly, and the paper identifies the specific categories where LLM norm judgement breaks down.
use_in_consilient: Evidence for the design question 'can an LLM be the norm monitor?' — i.e. can the regulation half of ORA4MAS be implemented by a model rather than a symbolic checker. It says: sometimes, model-dependent, and you must measure it against human ground truth rather than assume it. That is directly our compliance-monitoring subsystem, and it establishes the methodology (multiple human annotators per scenario, per-norm breakdown) we should copy.
the_bar_it_sets: Small: 80 scenarios, 10 norms, 3 human annotators, three models, no inter-annotator agreement statistic reported and no per-norm error analysis at scale — the authors call it a pilot. We beat it easily on scale and rigour: more norms drawn from a real deontic specification rather than household commonsense, reported inter-annotator agreement, and detection recall/precision measured on live agent traces rather than authored stories.
verified_how: Fetched https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.16517 directly; the abstract page returned the exact title, all four authors, v1 25 March 2024 / v2 14 October 2024, the comment field stating 'To appear in COINE@AAMAS-2024 Springer LNCS post-proceedings', and the abstract with the 80-scenario / 10-norm / 3-evaluator detail.

title: Prompt Engineering Guide — Agents section (Introduction, Components, AI Workflows vs AI Agents)
authors_or_lab: Elvis Saravia / DAIR.AI
venue_year: dair.ai, continuously updated; agents section live as of Aug 2026
reputable_because: DAIR.AI, named explicitly by the principal as an admissible source. The Prompt Engineering Guide is DAIR.AI's flagship publication (8M+ learners claimed on dair.ai homepage).
what_it_establishes: DAIR.AI's own agent taxonomy is a three-component model, not a loop model. Instrument the self-directed learner with a two-number gauge per self-generated artefact (skill, tool, note, dataset): (a) novelty = surprisal of the artefact under the agent's own pre-artefact predictor, (b) learnability = drop in that predictor's loss on held-out sibling tasks after the artefact is admitted. Admit to the skill/context library only if BOTH are positive. This directly kills the two degenerate modes below (repetition = zero novelty; hallucinated junk = zero learnability).
the_bar_it_sets: Any "the agent improves itself when idle" claim must be accompanied by the novelty×learnability curve over wall-clock, not a benchmark delta. It is a single integer that cannot be gamed by generating more tasks (novelty gate) or by generating easier ones (solve gate must use exogenous verification). title: Self-Improvement in Language Models: The Sharpening Mechanism
authors_or_lab: Audrey Huang, Adam Block, Dylan J. Foster, Dhruv Rohatgi, Cyril Zhang, Max Simchowitz, Jordan T. Ash, Akshay Krishnamurthy — Microsoft Research (NYC), with UIUC and CMU
reputable_because: Microsoft Research — named frontier lab. Foster, Krishnamurthy, Ash, Block and Zhang are MSR NYC's RL theory group.
what_it_establishes: THE CEILING, stated formally. Self-improvement does not create information. It 'sharpens' the model onto sequences the model already assigns high self-verification score to — it amortises inference-time best-of-N search into the weights. Consequence: SFT-based self-improvement is sample-optimal only when the base model already has *coverage* of good responses; RL-based self-improvement can beat that bound only because online exploration removes the coverage requirement. No mechanism produces capability the base model could not reach with enough sampling.
use_in_consilient: This is the theoretical reason our ambient loop must reach outside the model. Any Consilient self-improvement component whose only signal is the model's own judgement is, provably, a sharpening operator — it will converge and stop. Design rule: separate the pipeline into (a) sharpening components, which we should expect to saturate and should budget accordingly, and (b) genuinely information-adding components (tool execution, real environments, fetched documents, user feedback). Label every ambient subsystem with which of the two it is; that labelling is itself the deliverable.
the_bar_it_sets: It sets a bar we must not claim to beat: no honest measurement can show unbounded self-improvement from self-verification alone. Our measurement obligation is to show, for each ambient subsystem, whether its gains persist past the sharpening horizon — and if they saturate, to say so rather than reporting the first-iteration delta.

title: Mind the Gap: Examining the Self-Improvement Capabilities of Large Language Models

what_it_establishes: Defines and measures the GENERATION–VERIFICATION GAP: the difference between a model's ability to produce a good answer and its ability to recognise one. Empirically, a variant of the gap scales monotonically with pre-training FLOPs — meaning weaker/smaller models have less headroom, and the gap is a measurable, model-specific quantity, not a constant.

Before enabling any self-improvement loop in Consilient, measure the generation–verification gap on that exact task distribution. If it is ≈0, the loop cannot help and should be disabled rather than run. Make it a precondition check in the ambient scheduler: a task family with a measured gap below threshold gets routed to exogenous verification or to a human, never to self-filtering.
the_bar_it_sets: They measure the gap across model families and tasks and show it predicts self-improvement gain. We beat it by making the gap a *runtime gating signal* rather than a post-hoc analysis — i.e. reporting that Consilient declined to self-improve on N task families because their measured gap was insufficient. Nobody in this literature reports declining to run the loop.

title: Does Reinforcement Learning Really Incentivize Reasoning Capacity in LLMs Beyond the Base Model?
authors_or_lab: Yang Yue, Zhiqi Chen, Rui Lu, Andrew Zhao, Zhaokai Wang, Shiji Song, Gao Huang — Tsinghua University (LeapLab), Shanghai Jiao Tong

what_it_establishes: COUNTER-EVIDENCE, and the cleanest measurement-honesty lesson here. RLVR-trained models beat their base models at pass@1 but are BEATEN by the base model at large k on pass@k. So RLVR is narrowing the output distribution onto paths the base model already had — increasing sampling efficiency while *reducing* the reasoning boundary. Six popular RLVR algorithms behave alike and all remain far from exploiting the base model's potential. The apparent improvement is an artefact of measuring at k=1.
use_in_consilient: Mandates our evaluation protocol. Any Consilient self-improvement result must be reported as a pass@k curve across k, not a single-sample score, because single-sample scores systematically flatter distribution-narrowing methods. Add this as a standing rule in the measurement layer: k=1 deltas without the curve are not admissible evidence of improvement.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is a self-improvement loop whose pass@k curve does not cross below the base model at any k — i.e. gains in efficiency without loss of reach. Almost nothing in the literature demonstrates this. If Consilient's ambient loop can show a non-crossing curve, that is a genuinely novel, publishable measurement.

title: AI models collapse when trained on recursively generated data
authors_or_lab: Ilia Shumailov, Zakhar Shumaylov, Yiren Zhao, Nicolas Papernot, Ross Anderson, Yarin Gal — Oxford (Gal, Shumailov), Cambridge (Shumaylov, the late Ross Anderson), Imperial, Toronto/Vector (Papernot)
reputable_because: Nature — the Nature/Science family is explicitly on the approved venue list. Authors from Oxford and Cambridge, both on the approved lab list.
what_it_establishes: THE definitive peer-reviewed counter-evidence. Training generatively on recursively generated data causes irreversible defects. Two distinct phases: EARLY collapse, where the model loses the tails of the distribution and distributional error accumulates; and LATE collapse, where low-frequency events disappear permanently and the model converges to a low-variance point mass unlike the original distribution. The effect is not a training bug — it follows from finite sampling, and it is irreversible once tails are lost.
use_in_consilient: Hard constraint on the persistent skill/experience library. Every artefact the ambient loop writes back is, by construction, self-generated data that future sessions condition on. Mitigations to build in: (1) never let self-generated context fully displace original sources — retain provenance tags and always keep the real artefact reachable; (2) monitor tail diversity of the library (entropy / distinct-n over admitted artefacts) as a collapse alarm, because the early-collapse signature is tail loss BEFORE mean quality drops; (3) accumulate rather than replace.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is any long-running self-conditioning system that demonstrates *no* tail loss over generations. We beat it by publishing the library's diversity-over-time curve alongside its capability curve — the collapse literature's core finding is that these two curves diverge, and the capability curve is the one everyone reports.
verified_how: Confirmed the paper exists at https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-024-07566-y (Nature vol 631, pp 755–759, 2024) and is indexed on PubMed (PMID 39048682) and the Edinburgh institutional repository. Authors and both-phase collapse finding confirmed.

title: Self-Consuming Generative Models Go MAD
authors_or_lab: Sina Alemohammad, Josue Casco-Rodriguez, Lorenzo Luzi, Ahmed Imtiaz Humayun, Hossein Babaei, Daniel LeJeune, Ali Siahkoohi, Richard G. Baraniuk — Rice University DSP group
reputable_because: ICLR 2024 — named peer-reviewed venue, with the proceedings PDF publicly hosted. Baraniuk's Rice DSP lab.
what_it_establishes: The taxonomy the collapse field now uses. Three autophagous ('self-consuming') loop regimes, distinguished by data supply: FULLY SYNTHETIC (no fresh real data), SYNTHETIC AUGMENTATION (fixed real set reused forever), and FRESH DATA (new real data each generation). Only the fresh-data regime avoids Model Autophagy Disorder (MAD). Critically: the first two regimes progressively lose either quality OR diversity, and *biasing sampling toward quality accelerates the loss of diversity* — you cannot trade your way out. Fixed real data merely delays MAD; it does not prevent it.
use_in_consilient: Classify the ambient loop into one of these three regimes explicitly and say which, in the docs. A self-directed agent generating skills from its own past sessions with no new external input is regime 1 and will go MAD. The design requirement this imposes: the idle loop must have a fresh-real-data intake — new repositories, new docs, new user interactions, new tool outputs — per cycle, not merely a fixed corpus. Also: the quality/diversity trade result means any 'only keep the best self-generated skills' filter is actively accelerating diversity collapse, so the admission filter must have an explicit diversity term.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is demonstrating which regime a system is in and showing the corresponding degradation curve. We beat it by making the fresh-data rate a first-class, reported quantity of the ambient loop (bytes/artefacts of genuinely external input per self-generated artefact) — a ratio nobody currently publishes.
verified_how: Confirmed via the ICLR 2024 proceedings PDF at proceedings.iclr.cc (paper file ebc042e767de551803ccfcc45e2454f5) and the Rice DSP lab's own project page dsp.rice.edu/ai-loops/. arXiv id 2307.01850, author list confirmed.

title: Agent Workflow Memory

reputable_because: CMU (Neubig, Fried) and MIT CSAIL (Mao) — both named in the approved lab list.
what_it_establishes: A persistent, cross-session skill library that measurably works, with an important design choice: it induces reusable *workflows* (abstracted routines) from prior trajectories rather than storing raw trajectories. Two transferable lessons: (1) store abstracted workflows, not transcripts — the abstraction step is what makes memory generalise rather than overfit; (2) the online/no-training-split variant is the one that matches our ambient setting, and it is the variant where gains grow as distributions diverge, i.e. memory pays off most on unfamiliar work — the opposite of the usual retrieval story.
the_bar_it_sets: +24.6% / +51.1% relative success and 8.9–14.0 points under distribution shift, with reduced step counts. We beat it by measuring library *cost* as well as benefit — AWM reports gains but not memory growth rate, retrieval precision, or the point at which the library's context cost exceeds its benefit. what_it_establishes: An agent that autonomously gathers experience across a set of training tasks and extracts natural-language *insights* from them (notably by comparing success/failure pairs), then retrieves those insights at inference. We beat it by testing whether the accumulated insights survive a distribution change — ExpeL shows accumulation helps in-domain; whether an insight library transfers or actively misleads on a new domain is unmeasured, and is precisely the risk for a long-lived agent.

title: Nested Learning: The Illusion of Deep Learning Architectures

reputable_because: Google Research — frontier lab — and NeurIPS 2025, a named peer-reviewed venue. Verified on Google's own research blog.
what_it_establishes: Reframes a model as a set of nested optimisation problems running at DIFFERENT UPDATE FREQUENCIES, unifying architecture and optimiser as levels of one learning system. Argues catastrophic forgetting persists because architecture and optimisation are designed separately. The proof-of-concept 'Hope' architecture with a continuum memory system reports lower perplexity and higher common-sense-reasoning accuracy than Titans, Samba and standard Transformers, and beats TTT and Mamba2 on long-context needle-in-a-haystack variants at three difficulty levels.

Structure the persistent store as tiers with explicit, different update rates: fast (this session's scratch), medium (per-project skills, updated per run), slow (cross-project principles, updated rarely and only on repeated evidence). Catastrophic forgetting in an agent memory shows up as the slow tier being churned by fast-tier noise; separating the update frequencies is the fix, and the tier's update rate is a settable, auditable parameter.
the_bar_it_sets: Beats Titans/Samba/Transformer on perplexity and Mamba2/TTT on long-context retrieval, with forgetting mitigation as the stated goal. We do not compete on architecture. We beat it in scope by applying multi-timescale updating to a *textual, human-auditable* memory and reporting per-tier churn rate and per-tier retention over months — an interpretability property no architectural approach offers.

title: Restless Bandits: Activity Allocation in a Changing World
authors_or_lab: P. Whittle (Churchill Professor of Mathematics for Operational Research, University of Cambridge)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Journal of Applied Probability; Whittle held the Churchill Chair at Cambridge, which is on the approved top-tier list. This is the founding paper of the restless-bandit field.
what_it_establishes: Defines the restless multi-armed bandit: N projects, at most M activated per timestep, and — crucially — the un-activated arms KEEP EVOLVING rather than freezing (the distinguishing feature versus Gittins). Whittle derives an index via Lagrangian relaxation of the hard 'exactly M active' constraint into an average constraint, priced by a subsidy-for-passivity λ. The index of an arm is the subsidy λ at which activating and not activating are equally attractive. Policy: activate the M arms of highest index. Whittle also notes indexability is not automatic — the passive set must grow monotonically in λ.
use_in_consilient: This is the direct formal model for the loop scheduler. Each background loop is an arm; its state is (time since last run, staleness of what it watches, accumulated unprocessed reactive load). Loops not run keep drifting — that is exactly restlessness, and it is why a plain Gittins/UCB scheduler is the wrong tool. The Lagrange multiplier λ IS the quota price: set λ high when remaining quota is scarce relative to time-to-reset, and low (even negative, i.e. paying to run) when quota is about to expire unused. One scalar knob turns the whole schedule from conservative to opportunistic. Compute a Whittle index per loop, run the top M that fit the current token budget.
the_bar_it_sets: Any scheduler we ship must be at least index-decomposable: a per-loop scalar priority computable from that loop's own state, with a single global price coupling them. If our scheduler needs joint reasoning over all loops, we have built something more expensive than 1988 state of the art without showing it beats it. Measurement that shows we beat it: simulate the loop fleet against a logged quota trace and compare cumulative value-delivered per token against a Whittle-index baseline; we must also report whether our index is indexable (passive set monotone in λ) or admit it is a heuristic.

title: On an Index Policy for Restless Bandits
authors_or_lab: Richard R. Weber (University of Cambridge, Statistical Laboratory) and Gideon Weiss
venue_year: Journal of Applied Probability 27, 637–648, 1990 (plus Addendum, Advances in Applied Probability 23, 429–430, 1991)
reputable_because: Peer-reviewed Journal of Applied Probability; Weber is at the Cambridge Statistical Laboratory, on the approved list.
what_it_establishes: The theoretical warrant for actually using the Whittle index. Shows that under an indexability condition plus a condition on the differential equation governing the fluid limit, the Whittle index policy is asymptotically optimal as the number of arms grows with a fixed activation fraction. The addendum matters as much as the paper: it corrects/qualifies the result, showing the required condition is not automatic and the index policy is NOT optimal in general. So: strong performance in the many-arms limit, no optimality guarantee for small N.

The scheduler should therefore ship with an explicit note in the ADR that the Whittle index is a heuristic at our fleet size, plus a measured comparison against an exact finite-horizon solve on a small instance so we know the size of the gap rather than assuming it away.
the_bar_it_sets: We may not claim optimality for an index scheduler. The bar is: state the asymptotic regime, state that we are not in it, and measure the actual suboptimality gap on a small instance (say 6 loops, 20-step horizon) where dynamic programming is tractable. If the gap is under a few percent of achievable value, the index is justified empirically; if not, we owe a different algorithm.

title: The Complexity of Optimal Queuing Network Control

title: Principles of Metareasoning
authors_or_lab: Stuart Russell and Eric Wefald (UC Berkeley)
reputable_because: Artificial Intelligence is the flagship peer-reviewed AI journal; Russell is at UC Berkeley, on the approved list. This is the paper that names and formalises metareasoning.
what_it_establishes: Formalises the value of computation: a deliberation step is worth taking only if its expected effect on the eventual decision, valued in outcome terms, exceeds its time/resource cost. Decisions about computation are themselves decisions under uncertainty and can be made rationally. Introduces the myopic single-step assumption that makes this tractable, and applies it to search control in game playing.
use_in_consilient: This is the missing conceptual spine for the whole loop-scheduling subsystem, and the brief is right that it is absent from our bibliography. It gives the correct objective function: a loop iteration should run iff E[change in the decision or artefact it informs] × value > token cost. That reframes 'should this loop run' from a scheduling question into a value-of-computation question, and it gives the numerator for the Whittle index in finding #1 — the index needs a value term, and this is where that term comes from rather than being invented.
the_bar_it_sets: A 25-year-old paper already requires that we estimate the expected VALUE of a computation before spending on it. A scheduler that only tracks cost and staleness — with no estimate of what the run will change — is below the 1991 bar. Measurement: log, per loop run, whether the run altered any downstream artefact or decision; a loop whose empirical P(changes anything) is near zero should have a near-zero index, and we should be able to show the scheduler learned that.

title: Optimal Composition of Real-Time Systems
authors_or_lab: Shlomo Zilberstein (UMass Amherst) and Stuart Russell (UC Berkeley)
reputable_because: Artificial Intelligence journal, peer-reviewed flagship; Russell at Berkeley (approved list), Zilberstein is the definitive author on anytime algorithms.
what_it_establishes: How to compose a system out of multiple anytime components each having its own performance profile (quality as a function of allocated time), and how to allocate a global time budget across those components optimally. Introduces conditional performance profiles and a compilation step that solves the allocation offline so the runtime decision is cheap.
use_in_consilient: This is the composition problem we actually have and have not named: Consilient is not one loop, it is several loops each of which is itself an anytime process (a shallower or deeper pass produces a worse or better result). Zilberstein–Russell says the right object is a per-loop performance profile — value as a function of tokens spent — and that the fleet-level budget split should be computed from those profiles, not from fixed per-loop caps. A scheduler that treats each loop as a fixed-cost atom is below this bar because it cannot trade depth-within-a-loop against breadth-across-loops. Measurement: show a curve of output quality vs tokens for at least one loop, and show the scheduler exploiting its concavity — i.e. that it stops deepening one loop where marginal value falls below another loop's marginal value.

title: Monitoring and Control of Anytime Algorithms: A Dynamic Programming Approach

reputable_because: Artificial Intelligence journal, peer-reviewed flagship. Zilberstein's UMass RBR lab is the canonical source on anytime-algorithm control.
what_it_establishes: Solves the stopping problem rather than the allocation problem: given an anytime computation in progress, when do you stop and act? Handles three sources of uncertainty at once — uncertainty in the algorithm's own progress, uncertainty in the environment, and, importantly, the cost of monitoring itself. Yields a dynamic-programming solution and shows that monitoring should be non-myopic and can be worth doing only intermittently, because checking progress is not free.

And the monitoring-cost result is the specific insight we would otherwise miss: if the scheduler asks an LLM 'is this loop making progress?' each cycle, the meta-query burns the same quota it is trying to conserve. title: Bandits with Knapsacks
authors_or_lab: Ashwinkumar Badanidiyuru (Google Research), Robert Kleinberg (Cornell), Aleksandrs Slivkins (Microsoft Research)

reputable_because: JACM is peer-reviewed and about as strong as computer science venues get; FOCS likewise. Authors at Microsoft Research (approved frontier lab) and Cornell.
what_it_establishes: The formal model for exploration under a hard, exhaustible budget: each pull costs a resource-dependent amount, the process halts when any budget is exhausted, and the learner must trade information against depletion. Gives algorithms with near-optimal regret against the best fixed distribution over arms, and shows the optimal policy is generally a MIXTURE of arms rather than a single best arm — a structural fact that pure UCB-style reasoning misses.
use_in_consilient: This is the piece the restless-bandit framing does not give us: a hard budget that ends the episode. A subscription quota is exactly a knapsack — the 5-hour or weekly window terminates when tokens run out, not when the clock does. Two direct consequences for our scheduler. (1) The optimal quota allocation is a randomised mixture over loops, so a deterministic 'always run the highest-index loop' policy is provably the wrong shape near the budget boundary. Measurement: replay a quota window offline, compute the best fixed mixture in hindsight, and report the gap. If the gap does not shrink with budget, our learner is not learning.

Log-linear coverage means the marginal value of the Nth loop iteration decays roughly as 1/N — that is a concrete, fittable functional form for the index's value term, far better than a guessed constant. The negative result is the load-bearing one for us: for any loop whose output has no automatic verifier, extra iterations stop paying, so the scheduler should cap unverifiable loops hard and spend the saved quota on verifiable ones.

title: s1: Simple Test-Time Scaling

what_it_establishes: Budget forcing: a mechanism for CONTROLLING inference spend by either terminating generation early or forcing it to continue. This is the control-side complement to the scaling laws — it demonstrates that a hard token budget can be imposed on a reasoning process from outside and that quality varies monotonically and predictably with the budget you set. s1-32B, trained on only 1,000 curated examples, exceeds o1-preview on competition maths by up to 27% and reaches 57% on AIME24 under extended budget.

Findings #1–#10 tell the scheduler what budget each loop should get; budget forcing is how you make a loop actually respect that number rather than running until it decides to stop. Consilient's loop runner should take a token budget as a first-class argument and enforce it by truncation-or-extension, so the scheduler's decision is binding. Without an enforceable budget, an optimal allocation is advisory and quota still gets burned.
the_bar_it_sets: Budgets must be enforced, not suggested. The bar: for every loop run, measured token spend must fall within a stated tolerance of the scheduler's allocation, and the quality-vs-budget relationship must be monotone. Measurement: log allocated vs actual tokens per run and report the distribution of overruns. Any loop that routinely exceeds its allocation makes the entire scheduling layer fictional and should be reported as a defect, not tuned away quietly.

title: Language Model Cascades: Token-Level Uncertainty and Beyond
authors_or_lab: Neha Gupta, Harikrishna Narasimhan, Wittawat Jitkrittum, Ankit Singh Rawat, Aditya Krishna Menon, Sanjiv Kumar (Google Research)
reputable_because: Google Research (approved frontier lab) and ICLR (approved peer-reviewed venue), confirmed via DBLP.
what_it_establishes: How to build the deferral rule in a cost-aware cascade for GENERATIVE models, where the naive approach breaks. Sequence-level uncertainty suffers a length bias — longer generations look more uncertain regardless of correctness — so deferring on sequence uncertainty systematically escalates the wrong requests. Fix: use token-level uncertainty features with a learned post-hoc deferral rule, optionally combining small-model embeddings and large-model intermediate layers. Improves the cost-quality Pareto frontier across NLP benchmarks on FLAN-T5.
use_in_consilient: The specific mechanism for spending less per loop iteration without a quality cliff: run the cheap model first, escalate to the expensive one only when a learned deferral rule says the cheap answer is untrustworthy. The length-bias finding is the concrete trap to avoid — Consilient's loop outputs vary enormously in length, so any 'escalate when the model seems unsure' heuristic built on whole-output confidence will misroute exactly the long outputs that matter most. Build the deferral rule on token-level signals and train it post-hoc on logged runs.
the_bar_it_sets: The deliverable is a cost-quality Pareto curve, not a single operating point: for each cascade threshold, plot achieved quality against tokens spent, and show our curve dominates both always-cheap and always-expensive. We must also explicitly test our deferral rule for length bias — bucket by output length and show the deferral rate is not simply tracking length.

title: SpotServe: Serving Generative Large Language Models on Preemptible Instances
authors_or_lab: Xupeng Miao, Chunan Shi, Jiangfei Duan, Xiaoli Xi, Dahua Lin, Bin Cui, Zhihao Jia (Zhihao Jia's Catalyst group, Carnegie Mellon University; with Peking University and CUHK)
reputable_because: CMU is on the approved top-tier lab list; ASPLOS is a top-tier peer-reviewed systems venue.
what_it_establishes: That systematically harvesting cheap-but-revocable capacity is a real, measurable win rather than a hazard to be avoided. SpotServe dynamically re-plans its parallelisation as instances appear and vanish, treats instance migration as a bipartite matching problem solved with Kuhn–Munkres, and adds stateful inference recovery so a preempted request resumes rather than restarts. The structural analogy is exact: quota remaining in a window that will reset is capacity that is free-if-used and worthless-if-not — the same economics as a spot instance, inverted in time. Two transferable mechanisms: (1) work must be preemption-tolerant, i.e. every opportunistic loop run must checkpoint so that hitting the quota wall truncates rather than destroys it, which is SpotServe's stateful recovery; (2) the burst plan should be recomputed as capacity changes rather than fixed at window start. Concretely: near a reset, drain a queue of low-priority deferred work whose runs are individually cheap and individually abandonable.
the_bar_it_sets: 54% cost saving from harvesting otherwise-wasted capacity is the reference figure, and it comes with a latency cost that the paper reports rather than hides. Our bar: measure quota utilisation (tokens used / tokens available per window) before and after opportunistic drain, and report the harm as well as the gain — specifically whether opportunistic work ever displaced reactive user-facing work. A saving that came from starving the user is a regression reported as a win.

Consilient beats it by making the accountability terminus machine-checkable: no action executes unless it resolves to a live human accountable party, measured as the fraction of executed actions with a resolvable accountable principal (target 100%, and report the misses).

The typed authority link is the piece most agent frameworks lack: it says which role may legitimately instruct which other role, so a lateral agent cannot commandeer a peer.

Consilient beats it by enforcing the deontic layer at runtime and measuring unfulfilled obligations — count of role-obligations that expired unmet per run, which is the honest measure of whether an agent org actually did its job, as opposed to whether it merely avoided doing forbidden things.

title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
authors_or_lab: Joon Sung Park, Joseph C. O'Brien, Carrie J. Cai, Meredith Ringel Morris, Percy Liang, Michael S. Bernstein — Stanford HCI/NLP with Google Research
reputable_because: Stanford HCI Group + Percy Liang (Stanford CRFM); published at ACM UIST 2023, a peer-reviewed venue. Co-authors at Google Research.
what_it_establishes: The canonical architecture for TRIGGERED (not requested) recall. A raw append-only memory stream of natural-language observations is scored automatically on every action cycle by a weighted sum of recency (exponential decay, factor 0.995 per hour), importance (LLM-rated 1-10 poignancy) and relevance (embedding cosine to the current situation); top-k is injected before the agent reasons. Reflection synthesises higher-level assertions periodically when summed importance of recent events crosses a threshold. Ablation is the load-bearing result: removing memory, reflection or planning each measurably degraded believability ratings in a controlled human evaluation, with full architecture > no-reflection > no-reflection-no-planning > no-memory. The agent never issues a retrieval query.
use_in_consilient: Directly replaces the retrieval policy in src/consilient/recall.py. Today `pack(log_dir, query=..., limit_chars=...)` does token-overlap matching against a caller-supplied query string plus a hardcoded ALWAYS_INCLUDE_KINDS set — i.e. requested recall with a crude always-on override. Generative Agents gives the three-term scoring function to replace both: recency decay over event timestamps, an importance field written at event-append time, and relevance against the current work item. The ALWAYS_INCLUDE_KINDS frozenset is the degenerate case of importance=max.
the_bar_it_sets: Any triggered-recall design must beat a three-term recency/importance/relevance score, and must be able to show an ablation table where removing each term degrades a measured outcome. We beat it by showing that on a held-out set of Consilient trajectories, our scorer surfaces the event a human judge marks as decisive at higher rate@k than the 2023 scorer — and that the recency half-life is fitted from our own event log rather than borrowed at 0.995/hour.

title: An integrated theory of the mind (ACT-R 5.0/6.0)
authors_or_lab: John R. Anderson, Daniel Bothell, Michael D. Byrne, Scott Douglass, Christian Lebiere, Yulin Qin — Carnegie Mellon University
reputable_because: CMU (Anderson's ACT-R lab); Psychological Review is a top peer-reviewed journal. 3,242 citations per Semantic Scholar. FOUNDATIONAL EXCEPTION under rule 4 — this is 22 years old and is the reason it matters: it is the formal specification of triggered retrieval, and it is absent from our bibliography.
what_it_establishes: Declarative memory retrieval in ACT-R is never requested by the reasoner. A retrieval request is a pattern placed in a buffer; the chunk that wins is the one with highest activation A_i = B_i + Σ W_j S_ji + ε, where B_i is base-level activation decaying as a power law of time since each past use (log Σ t_k^-d, d≈0.5), and Σ W_j S_ji is spreading activation from whatever is currently in the goal/context buffers. A retrieval threshold τ means low-activation chunks are simply not returned — the failure is silent and typed, not an empty result set. Latency is exponential in activation. Every constant here was fitted against human reaction-time and fMRI data across dozens of tasks.
use_in_consilient: Gives us a memory-scoring formula with 25 years of empirical fitting behind it, and two things Generative Agents lacks: (a) spreading activation — an event becomes retrievable because it is *associated with* something in the current context, not because it lexically matches, which is exactly what recall.py's `_searchable_text` token overlap cannot do; (b) a retrieval threshold, so 'no memory was relevant' is a first-class outcome rather than a bottom-k pack of noise. Base-level decay is the forgetting policy: nothing is deleted, activation falls below τ.
the_bar_it_sets: A memory system that cannot express 'this event is relevant because it is associated with the current ticket, though it shares no tokens with it' is behind 2004. The measurement that shows we beat it: fit d (decay exponent) and τ (threshold) on our own trajectory log, then show retrieval-precision at fixed pack size beats both flat recency and pure lexical match — and report the abstention rate, which lexical match cannot produce.

title: A Standard Model of the Mind: Toward a Common Computational Framework across Artificial Intelligence, Cognitive Science, Neuroscience, and Robotics

The adaptive policy (retrieve only when the subject entity's popularity falls below a threshold) improves accuracy AND cuts inference cost simultaneously. It gives us the shape of the trigger predicate: retrieve when the model's own prior is weak, not on every turn. For Consilient the analogue of 'entity popularity' is how routine the work item is — a dispatch pattern the agent has executed a hundred times needs no recall pack; a novel one does. This is a cheap, non-LLM trigger we can compute from the projection.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
authors_or_lab: Nelson F. Liu, Kevin Lin, John Hewitt, Ashwin Paranjape, Michele Bevilacqua, Fabio Petroni, Percy Liang — Stanford NLP (Percy Liang) with Samaya AI / Meta
reputable_because: Stanford NLP / CRFM (Percy Liang, John Hewitt); Transactions of the ACL is a peer-reviewed journal.
what_it_establishes: Where you put the surfaced memory changes whether the model uses it. Across multi-document QA and key-value retrieval, accuracy is highest when the relevant item sits at the start or end of the context and degrades substantially when it sits in the middle — a U-shaped curve. The effect persists in models explicitly built for long context, so it is not fixed by a bigger window.
use_in_consilient: An implementation constraint on the recall pack, not an argument against it. recall.py assembles a bounded markdown pack ordered by event log order and truncates with an omitted-count footer — which means the highest-scoring memory can land in the middle and be effectively ignored. The fix is ordering by score into the head and tail positions rather than chronologically, and it costs almost nothing. (2) The staged filter cascade (cheap syntactic filters first, expensive semantic matching last) is the right cost structure for a large catalogue. title: The Contract Net Protocol: High-Level Communication and Control in a Distributed Problem Solver
authors_or_lab: Reid G. Smith (work conducted at Stanford University)
venue_year: IEEE Transactions on Computers, C-29(12):1104–1113, December 1980
reputable_because: IEEE Transactions on Computers — a peer-reviewed venue (rule 1). RETURNED DELIBERATELY UNDER RULE 4: this is the foundational work of the organisational multi-agent systems literature the brief identifies as a 25-year blind spot in our bibliography.
what_it_establishes: Defines task allocation by negotiation: a manager node ANNOUNCES a task, capable nodes evaluate the announcement against their own state and submit BIDS, the manager AWARDS a contract, and the contractor may itself decompose and re-announce. Allocation is therefore decided by mutual selection under local information, with no central allocator and no requirement that the manager know the full capability inventory in advance.
use_in_consilient: This is the alternative to retrieval that our whole design space is currently ignoring. Every modern approach — embedding retrieval, generative tool tokens, progressive filesystem disclosure — makes the CALLER responsible for finding the right tool from a catalogue it must first index. Contract Net inverts it: broadcast the task, let tools/agents that can serve it bid with their own cost and confidence estimates, and select on bids. For Consilient specifically this handles the case retrieval handles worst — a user connects a tool mid-session that no index has seen, and it can still bid. It also gives a natural, honest place to put COST: a paid connector's bid can carry its price, so the free/open-source path wins by default unless a paid tool bids materially better, which is exactly the preference ordering the design goal states.
the_bar_it_sets: Forty-six years old and it already solves dynamic capability allocation without a central catalogue. The bar: Consilient must justify why it is doing retrieval at all rather than bidding, or run both. The measurement that would settle it — on a catalogue with tools appearing and disappearing at runtime, compare retrieval-based selection against a bidding protocol on selection accuracy, latency and cost-of-tool-used. If bidding wins on newly-added tools, that is a genuinely novel result for the MCP era and it comes from reading 1980.

title: Debating with More Persuasive LLMs Leads to More Truthful Answers
authors_or_lab: Akbir Khan, John Hughes, Dan Valentine, Laura Ruis, Edward Grefenstette, Tim Rocktäschel (UCL); Kshitij Sachan, Ansh Radhakrishnan, Samuel R. Bowman, Ethan Perez (Anthropic)
venue_year: ICML 2024 (PMLR v235); arXiv Feb 2024, v4 Jul 2024
reputable_because: Anthropic co-authorship (Perez, Bowman, Sachan, Radhakrishnan) — a frontier lab on the allowed list — plus UCL. Published in Proceedings of the 41st ICML, Volume 235, a listed peer-reviewed venue.
what_it_establishes: Two expert models debate opposing answers on QuALITY reading comprehension while a non-expert judge who has NOT seen the source article decides. Debate raises non-expert model accuracy to 76% and human accuracy to 88%, against naive baselines of 48% and 60% respectively. Optimising debaters for persuasiveness in an unsupervised manner further improves the non-expert's ability to identify truth — i.e. the gain does not require ground-truth labels.
use_in_consilient: This is the closest thing to a direct test of the project's load-bearing claim available from a frontier lab. The mechanism producing the gain is not model diversity — both debaters are the same model — it is EVIDENCE asymmetry: debaters can cite verified quotes from a passage the judge cannot see. Consilient's aggregator should therefore be built as a judge deliberately deprived of the raw evidence, consuming only agent-supplied verified citations, because that deprivation is what makes the agreement informative rather than echoic.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is a 28-point lift (48% to 76%) for a non-expert judge over its own unaided baseline, using same-model debaters. Consilient must show that its evidence-routing produces a comparable judge-side lift, and must run the same-model ablation to prove the gain is not coming from model heterogeneity. If Consilient cannot beat 76% on an equivalent asymmetric-evidence task with same-model agents, the evidence-diversity thesis is not yet operationalised.

NOTE: I have seen this described elsewhere as an ICML 2024 best paper; the PMLR page notes no award, so I do NOT assert that. Id absent from the cited list.

title: On scalable oversight with weak LLMs judging strong LLMs
authors_or_lab: Zachary Kenton, Noah Y. Siegel, János Kramár, Jonah Brown-Cohen, Samuel Albanie, Jannis Bulian, Rishabh Agarwal, David Lindner, Yunhao Tang, Noah D. Goodman, Rohin Shah — Google DeepMind
reputable_because: Google DeepMind — a frontier lab explicitly on the allowed list (Kenton, Kramár, Shah, Lindner are DeepMind scalable-oversight team; Goodman is Stanford).
what_it_establishes: Compares debate, consultancy, and direct QA with LLM judges weaker than the debaters, across extractive QA, closed QA, maths, coding, logic and multimodal tasks. Two findings matter here. First: 'debate outperforms consultancy across all tasks when the consultant is randomly assigned to argue for the correct/incorrect answer.' Second, and decisive for us: 'In extractive QA tasks with information asymmetry, debate outperforms QA without article... but not QA with article. For other tasks, when the judge is weaker than the debaters (but not too weak), we find either small or no advantage to debate over QA without article.' The asymmetry is defined explicitly: the article is 'supplied to consultants/debaters but not to the judge, introducing an information asymmetry.'
use_in_consilient: This is the single most load-bearing finding in the whole search, and it is a frontier-lab result that CONFIRMS the project's thesis in its strong form: debate's advantage exists only where agents hold evidence the judge lacks, and evaporates the moment the judge is given the article. That is precisely the ECHO-vs-consilience distinction, measured. Consilient's core invariant should be derived from this: a panel is only epistemically productive when the members' evidence sets differ from each other's and from the aggregator's. Instrument evidence-set overlap per run and treat high overlap as a signal that the panel is echoing and should collapse to a single agent.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is negative and sharp: on any task WITHOUT evidence asymmetry, debate gives 'small or no advantage'. Consilient must reproduce this null on symmetric-evidence tasks — if we report gains where DeepMind found none, that is evidence of a measurement bug or benchmark leakage, not of a better architecture. To show we beat it we must demonstrate a monotone relationship between measured evidence-set divergence and panel gain, with gain at zero divergence indistinguishable from zero.

title: Rethinking the Bounds of LLM Reasoning: Are Multi-Agent Discussions the Key?
authors_or_lab: Qineng Wang, Zihao Wang, Ying Su, Yangqiu Song (HKUST); Hanghang Tong (UIUC)
venue_year: ACL 2024 (62nd Annual Meeting, Bangkok — Volume 1, Long Papers); arXiv Feb 2024
reputable_because: Published at ACL 2024 main conference, long paper — ACL is a listed peer-reviewed venue. (Affiliations HKUST/UIUC are not on the named-lab list; the venue is what qualifies it.)
what_it_establishes: Systematically compares multi-agent discussion frameworks against a single agent across reasoning tasks and models. Core result: 'a single-agent LLM with strong prompts can achieve almost the same performance as the best existing discussion approach.' The crucial conditional: multi-agent discussion only outperforms single-agent when the prompts lack demonstrations. In other words, the apparent multi-agent gain is largely a substitute for good prompting, and disappears once the single-agent baseline is made strong.
use_in_consilient: This is the baseline-strength trap, and it is the most common way a multi-agent result is manufactured. Consilient's evaluation protocol must mandate that the single-agent control is prompt-optimised to the same effort as the multi-agent system, with demonstrations included — otherwise every gain we report is confounded. Make 'strong-prompt single agent with demonstrations' a required control in the harness, not an optional one.
the_bar_it_sets: Consilient must beat a demonstration-equipped, strong-prompt single agent — not a naive zero-shot one. Measurement: report both controls side by side on every eval, and report the gap between them. If Consilient's advantage over the naive baseline is large but its advantage over the strong-prompt baseline is near zero, we have reproduced this paper's finding and must say so.

title: AI Agents That Matter
authors_or_lab: Sayash Kapoor, Benedikt Stroebl, Zachary S. Siegel, Nitya Nadgir, Arvind Narayanan — Princeton University (Center for Information Technology Policy / PLI)
reputable_because: Princeton (Narayanan, Kapoor) — a listed top-tier university lab.
what_it_establishes: Identifies five structural defects in agent evaluation. The load-bearing one: the field 'focuses on accuracy without attending to cost', which produces needlessly complex and expensive agent architectures whose apparent gains vanish once cost is controlled. Argues for jointly optimising accuracy and cost, shows that benchmark-specific overfitting is rife because many agent benchmarks lack proper holdout sets, and that evaluation is unstandardised and irreproducible. Proposes a principled framework for cost-controlled, overfitting-resistant agent evaluation.
use_in_consilient: This is the methodology spec for our evaluation harness, and it is the direct institutional expression of the repository's founding scepticism. Adopt the accuracy-cost Pareto frontier as the reporting primitive: Consilient results should never be reported as a single accuracy number. Also adopt their holdout discipline — a multi-agent architecture is exactly the kind of system that can overfit a benchmark by encoding task structure into role definitions.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is that a simple baseline must be plotted on the same accuracy-cost axes and Consilient must sit strictly above and to the left of it. Measurement showing we beat it: a Pareto plot where, at every cost level tested, Consilient's accuracy exceeds the best single-agent configuration at that cost — and a held-out task set the architecture was never tuned on.

title: Improving Multi-Agent Debate with Sparse Communication Topology
authors_or_lab: Yunxuan Li, Yibing Du, Jiageng Zhang, Le Hou, Peter Grabowski, Yeqing Li, Eugene Ie — Google
reputable_because: Google (Le Hou, Eugene Ie, Peter Grabowski — Google Research/DeepMind) — a frontier lab on the allowed list.
what_it_establishes: Points out that existing multi-agent debate work 'adopt[s] a brute force algorithm -- each agent can communicate with all other agents', and systematically varies communication connectivity. On GPT and Mistral models, 'multi-agent debates leveraging sparse communication topology can achieve comparable or superior performance while significantly reducing computational costs.' Extends the result to multimodal reasoning and alignment labelling.
use_in_consilient: Direct evidence that the default fully-connected panel is the wrong architecture and that pruning edges is free or better. For Consilient this is doubly interesting: sparsity limits how far one agent's framing can propagate, which is mechanically an anti-ECHO measure. Make sparse topology the default and treat all-to-all as the ablation, and measure whether the sparse configuration reduces cross-agent answer correlation as well as cost.
the_bar_it_sets: Consilient's topology must beat both dense debate AND this sparse variant on accuracy-per-token. Measurement: hold agent count fixed, vary edge density, and report both accuracy and pairwise agent-output correlation. If our chosen topology neither beats sparse on cost nor lowers correlation, the topology is arbitrary.
