title: Demystifying Multi-Agent Debate: The Role of Confidence and Diversity
authors_or_lab: Xiaochen Zhu, Caiqi Zhang, Nigel Collier, Andreas Vlachos (University of Cambridge); Yizhou Chi (UC Berkeley); Tom Stafford (University of Sheffield)
reputable_because: University of Cambridge (Nigel Collier, Andreas Vlachos) — a listed top-tier university lab.
what_it_establishes: States as its premise that 'recent work shows that vanilla MAD often underperforms simple majority vote despite higher computational cost' — a negative result about debate treated as established. Then isolates two variables that recover the gain: diversity-aware initialisation, which selects varied candidate answers specifically to raise the probability that a correct hypothesis is present in the pool at all, and a confidence-modulated protocol where agents express calibrated confidence. The combination 'consistently outperform[s] vanilla MAD and majority vote' across six reasoning QA benchmarks. Explicitly frames itself as bridging human deliberation research and LLM debate.
use_in_consilient: The most directly relevant recent test of the diversity claim in a debate setting. Its mechanism is worth stating precisely because it is subtly different from ours: the gain comes from ensuring the correct answer is REPRESENTED in the initial pool, and from calibrated confidence weighting the aggregation. That is diversity of hypotheses plus honest uncertainty — closer to our thesis than model-swapping, but still not evidence diversity. Consilient should adopt calibrated-confidence-weighted aggregation, and should adopt their control: measure whether the correct answer was present in the pool at all, separately from whether the panel selected it.
the_bar_it_sets: Two bars. The negative one: vanilla debate underperforms simple majority vote at higher cost — Consilient must beat majority vote at matched cost or it is worse than nothing. The positive one: diversity-aware init plus confidence modulation beats both across six QA benchmarks. To show evidence diversity is the real driver, Consilient must beat THIS system, whose diversity is hypothesis-level rather than evidence-level, on a task where the two come apart.

title: Chain of Agents: Large Language Models Collaborating on Long-Context Tasks
authors_or_lab: Yusen Zhang, Ruoxi Sun, Yanfei Chen, Tomas Pfister, Sercan Ö. Arik (Google); Rui Zhang (Penn State)
reputable_because: Google (Tomas Pfister, Sercan Arik — Google Cloud AI Research) — a frontier lab on the allowed list.
what_it_establishes: Multiple worker agents each process a different segment of a long document and communicate sequentially; a manager agent synthesises. Reports improvements 'by up to 10% over strong baselines of RAG, Full-Context, and multi-agent LLMs' across question answering, summarisation and code completion. Notably the baselines include full-context and other multi-agent systems, not just a naive single agent.
use_in_consilient: A clean example of the ONE condition under which multi-agent structure has an unarguable justification: the evidence physically does not fit in one context window, so agents necessarily hold disjoint evidence. This is the degenerate, easy case of the evidence-diversity thesis — the diversity is imposed by the token limit rather than chosen. Consilient should treat context overflow as an automatic trigger for fan-out, and should treat every other fan-out decision as requiring separate justification.
the_bar_it_sets: Up to 10% over full-context and RAG on long-context QA/summarisation. The harder bar it implies for us: Consilient must show a gain in the case where the evidence DOES fit in one window, because that is the case where structure is not forced by physics. A gain only in the overflow regime would mean Consilient is a chunking strategy, not an epistemic architecture.

title: MDAgents: An Adaptive Collaboration of LLMs for Medical Decision-Making
authors_or_lab: Yubin Kim, Chanwoo Park, Hyewon Jeong, Yik Siu Chan, Xuhai Xu, Marzyeh Ghassemi, Cynthia Breazeal, Hae Won Park (MIT); Daniel McDuff (Google); Hyeonhoon Lee (Seoul National University Hospital)
reputable_because: MIT (Media Lab — Breazeal, Hae Won Park; CSAIL/EECS — Marzyeh Ghassemi) — a listed top-tier university lab.
what_it_establishes: Dynamically assigns LLMs to SOLO or COLLABORATIVE structures depending on assessed medical task complexity, rather than always forming a group. Achieves best performance on seven of ten benchmarks with improvements up to 4.2% over prior methods; combining moderator review with external medical knowledge in group settings yields an average accuracy improvement of 11.8%.
use_in_consilient: The important contribution for us is not the 4.2% — it is that the system is built on the premise that group structure is only worth paying for on complex items, and it routes simple items to a single agent. That is exactly the discipline this repository is arguing for, implemented and measured in a high-stakes domain. Consilient should have an equivalent complexity gate in front of the panel, and should log how often the gate correctly declines to convene one. The 11.8% figure is also notable because the gain comes from adding EXTERNAL KNOWLEDGE to the group, not from the group itself — again pointing at evidence rather than structure.
the_bar_it_sets: Modest and honest: 4.2% over prior methods, best on 7 of 10 benchmarks. The bar Consilient must clear is the gate's accuracy, not the panel's — measure what fraction of items the complexity gate routes to solo, and show that forcing those items through the panel would have cost tokens without improving accuracy. If our gate never declines to convene, we have not implemented the lesson.

title: Evidence for a Collective Intelligence Factor in the Performance of Human Groups
authors_or_lab: Anita Williams Woolley (Carnegie Mellon), Christopher F. Chabris (Union College), Alex Pentland, Nada Hashmi, Thomas W. Malone (MIT)
reputable_because: Published in Science — the Nature/Science family is explicitly on the allowed list. Authors at CMU and MIT, both listed top-tier universities. RETURNED DELIBERATELY UNDER RULE 4: this is a foundational pre-2024 work that defines the field of measured group performance, and it is absent from the repository's bibliography. That absence is exactly the 25-year organisational blind spot the task names.
what_it_establishes: Establishes that a single statistical factor — 'c', collective intelligence — explains a group's performance across a wide range of tasks, in the same way g does for individuals. The findings that matter for this project: c is NOT strongly predicted by the average or maximum individual intelligence of the members. It is predicted instead by the average social sensitivity of members, by the EQUALITY OF CONVERSATIONAL TURN-TAKING (groups where a few people dominated discussion performed worse), and by the proportion of women in the group.
use_in_consilient: This is the empirical foundation for the claim that team performance is a property of the interaction protocol rather than of member quality — which is the whole premise of building an organisation out of agents rather than just buying a better model. Two directly implementable measurements: (1) instrument turn-taking equality across a Consilient panel and test whether skew predicts degraded output, exactly as it does in human groups; (2) test whether panel performance is predicted by the strongest member, because if it is, the panel is a router and should be replaced by one.
the_bar_it_sets: The bar is a structural one, not a number: Consilient must demonstrate a 'c-like' property — that panel performance is NOT explained by the best individual agent's solo performance. Measurement that would show we beat it: regress panel accuracy on best-member solo accuracy; a significant residual means the organisation is contributing something. No residual means we have built an expensive max() operator.

title: Groups of diverse problem solvers can outperform groups of high-ability problem solvers
authors_or_lab: Lu Hong (Loyola University Chicago), Scott E. Page (University of Michigan / Santa Fe Institute)
reputable_because: HONEST CAVEAT FIRST: this is the weakest source-provenance in my list. PNAS is a top-tier peer-reviewed journal but is not literally in the enumerated venue list, and Michigan/Loyola are not in the enumerated lab list. I am returning it under RULE 4 because it is the foundational formal result on the exact claim this repository is built on, it is absent from the bibliography, and no 2024-2026 paper I found supersedes it. Drop it if the venue rule is being read strictly.
what_it_establishes: A formal model plus computational experiment showing that a randomly selected group of diverse problem solvers can outperform a group composed of the individually highest-performing solvers. The mechanism is that high-ability solvers tend to share the same heuristics and therefore get stuck at the same local optima, whereas diverse solvers have non-overlapping stopping points and can unstick each other. This is the origin of the 'diversity trumps ability' theorem and, with Page's related diversity-prediction theorem, is the formal ancestor of every claim that heterogeneous ensembles beat homogeneous ones.
use_in_consilient: This is the theoretical statement of the project's founding principle, and it also states the precise failure condition: when solvers share heuristics they share local optima, and their agreement carries no information. Translated to LLMs, agents sharing a base model share heuristics, and agents sharing a retrieval corpus share evidence — both collapse to the homogeneous case. It gives Consilient a formal target: measure whether panel members get stuck at the same places, because overlapping stopping points is the operational definition of ECHO.
the_bar_it_sets: The theorem's conditions are the bar: the diversity advantage requires that solvers' local optima genuinely differ and that all solvers be individually competent. Consilient must show BOTH hold in our panels — measure inter-agent overlap of failure cases, not just of answers. If our agents fail on the same items, the theorem predicts no gain, and observing a gain anyway would indicate a measurement artefact. Note also that this is a model, not a measurement of real LLM agents; the honest use is as a hypothesis to test, never as a citation that our design works.
